sentences.gloss_en: Welcome; today we go deep into the world of real-time streaming.
Instead of mechanical theory, we follow one very practical journey: a single financial transaction.
In a Mobile Money system, from being logged in the Kafka log until it shows up in an executive's dashboard.
This journey will reveal the magic behind the scenes; let's start.
Today's six stations, quickly.
Three: the journey of our story's hero, the financial transaction.
Four: the components of the Next Gen Architecture.
Five: the four data flows.
And finally six: the dashboards, the SLAs and the invoices.
First station: the basics of streaming and Kafka.
To understand the picture we must tell two worlds apart.
On the left is batch processing: collecting data with a beginning and an end, processed once a day.
Its throughput is very high, but its latency, the delay, is also high.
On the right is the world of the stream: a river of events with no end.
Point after point they arrive and are processed in time, with latency almost nil.
Modern smart systems combine both in a Lambda Architecture: a fast real-time path and a batch path for reports.
What confuses many people is that Kafka is not an ordinary database at all; it is a log.
Imagine the topic split into horizontal partitions, with the producers dropping events at the end of each partition.
The consumer pointer moves forward reading, via sequential numbers called offsets.
The key point is that ordering is guaranteed only inside a single partition.
So if events depend on each other and must stay in order, they must take the same key to land in the same partition.
Here we reach the most important number in the life of anyone working in streaming: the lag.
Simply, it is the distance between the newest message that entered the platform and the last message the consumer managed to process.
A golden rule: the lag indicator must always be read and analyzed together with its cause in the same snapshot.
Because most of the time the problem is not in Kafka itself.
The problem is a sink, or a very slow downstream system at the end of the path, which delays the whole queue behind it.
Second station: failures, schemas and code.
Let's ask a question at the heart of it, one that tests the robustness of any system: what could happen?
If the consumer pulled a message, worked hard and processed it, but suddenly a crash happened.
The system went down before it could commit, or save its offset in the log.
When it comes back up again, what will happen?
When the consumer comes back to work it will read the same message again, and we will end up with a duplicate.
That is why the Exactly Once principle is not just a button you press in Kafka; it is a complete journey.
The practical and safer solution is to set the system to at least once.
And to receive the data in an idempotent sink, a smart sink that can swallow duplicates safely without spoiling the results.
And of course a poisoned message that keeps crashing the consumer is immediately moved to a dead letter queue, or DLQ, so the path keeps running and does not stop.
Looking at the code from inside, we find PySpark reading streams from port 9092.
It groups this data into time windows lasting five minutes, with a trigger every minute.
The key piece here is the watermark, which is set to ten minutes.
Meaning, the system gives late events ten minutes to arrive before it fully closes the window.
In the background the schema registry stands like a strict guard, rejecting any sudden change in data shape that could break the consumers.
Third station: the journey of the story's hero, the transaction.
Let's all focus on this number, TXN-99482, a real money transfer accurate to the piaster.
Someone pressed send, and the operating system recorded the amount and the parties and produced this lovely transaction number.
This number is the thread we will keep holding and tracking at every station inside our architecture, to show practically how real data moves.
At every hop inside the system, this transaction gets four stamps, at different times.
First, the time the event actually happened.
Then the time our platform received it; third, the processing time.
And fourth, the time it became available in a report we can see.
Mixing these times up and treating them as one is the trap that catches many people and creates differences in the numbers while we chase problems.
Fourth station: the components of the Next Gen Architecture inside the platform.
Data moves between levels; looking at the left we find the ODS layer, or the TO tables.
They stay very close to the shape of the original data at the source and are updated in near real time.
On the right we enter the ADS layer, or the TA tables.
Here we put our business logic and produce aggregated, calculated data ready for reports.
If we break down the components of Next Gen D&IM by function first and then product, we find the following.
For real-time event distribution we rely on Kafka, which carries up to 10,000 transactions per second.
For real-time processing our hero is Flink, and for batch and heavy reports, Spark.
For the APIs we use GaussDB.
The huge storage goes to HDFS, with a massive capacity reaching 352 terabytes.
The impressive part is that 13 different countries are connected to this platform.
Each country is completely isolated in its own databases.
The only thing that joins them is the Kafka bus, moving data at rocket speed.
Fifth station: the four data flows.
Data leaves this platform through four main paths, or flows.
First, Central Kafka, dedicated to heavy central systems such as fraud detection systems.
Second, Local Kafka, which serves each country's applications locally.
Third, API Out, which returns data as JSON with a maximum of one thousand records per request.
And fourth and last, the File Out path, the quiet nightly path that sends files over SFTP between 2 and 5 AM.
Sixth and last station: the dashboards, the SLAs and the invoices.
Let's live a day in the life of our heroine, the financial transaction.
The transfer happens, and within less than 5 minutes, which is our strict SLA.
The transaction shows up in the real-time report, and things calm down.
At night at 2 the heavy batch path begins.
Before 3 all the compliance files have been exported.
And by 5 in the early morning all the reports have been delivered to the downstream systems.
Every step here is measured to the second.
Central Kafka for example must finish within 70 seconds to 3 minutes, and the APIs within 5 to 15 minutes at most.
And now the moment of truth that proves the strength of this whole architecture.
Our same transaction number, TXN-99482, shows up lit on the executive management's dashboard screen.
Not a similar transaction nor an approximate aggregate, but exactly it.
This is the biggest proof that the data travelled from its tiny origin to the decision-making screens with utmost accuracy and transparency.
To confirm the business logic work in the ADS layer, we have six invoices recorded over the day.
The simple calculation says the successful total is 400 Egyptian pounds, split fairly.
The first operator gets 250 and the second operator gets 150.
The system classified the operations and by money produced a result accurate to the piaster.
From these invoices we derive the final statistic: four successful operations out of six.
Meaning the overall success rate for that day's transactions is 66.67%.
This is the crowning exact number of the long data journey inside the arteries of streaming and Kafka.
Before we end this explainer, we leave you with an important question to think about.
If we woke up one day and found a report delayed and the 5-minute freshness SLA broken.
I wonder, if we go back to the four time stamps we talked about.
Which stamp absorbed and created this delay: is it the ingestion time or the processing time?
The answer to this question is what separates pretty talk in presentations from real, professional engineering control over real time data.
Thank you very much for your time; we hope this tour lit up the picture inside the world of streaming.
Agenda item one: streaming and Kafka basics.
Agenda item two: failures, schemas and code.
